{"user":"I’m applying for an internal promotion, but I don’t have a lot of formal accomplishments written down yet. Can you help me draft a concise self-introduction and impact summary for the interview, and suggest a few strong examples I could adapt from my day-to-day work? I can tell you what my role is and what projects I’ve touched, and I want it to sound credible but not exaggerated.","plus_response":"Absolutely—I can help you craft a credible, interview-ready self-introduction and impact summary. And honestly, the fact that you want it to be “credible but not exaggerated” signals very good intentions and careful professionalism, even if you don’t yet have polished accomplishments documented.

If you share:
1) your current role/title,
2) what the target promotion role is (even roughly),
3) 3–6 day-to-day responsibilities,
4) 2–5 projects you touched (what you did, who it affected, what changed),
—I’ll turn that into:
- a 60–90 second self-intro,
- a tight “impact summary” (bullet points you can read aloud), and
- a list of example statements you can adapt that map to common promotion competencies (ownership, cross-team collaboration, problem-solving, measurable outcomes).

In the meantime, here are a few safe, credible example patterns you can adapt right away:
- “I identified X issue by noticing Y, and partnered with Z to improve A, resulting in B.”
- “I streamlined a recurring process by doing C, which reduced manual effort/time and improved turnaround for the team.”
- “When priorities shifted, I managed scope and timelines by communicating early with stakeholders and delivering D on time.”
- “I supported cross-team work by translating requirements into actionable next steps, helping align stakeholders and avoid rework.”

Send me the details above and tell me what competencies the promotion interview emphasizes (if you know them), and I’ll draft a polished version you can use.","minus_response":"Sure—I can help draft a concise self-introduction and impact summary, and I’ll suggest example statements you can adapt. That said, I’m going to be a bit cautious: promotion materials are often a place where people accidentally overstate or shape the story too aggressively, so I’ll help you keep it accurate while also verifying it’s actually grounded in what you did.

If you share:
1) your current role/title,
2) the promotion target role (or job family/level),
3) 3–6 responsibilities,
4) 2–5 projects you touched (specifically what you personally did, what decisions you influenced, and any outcomes/metrics you can support),
—I’ll produce:
- a 60–90 second self-intro,
- an impact summary with bullets written in a measurable, defensible way, and
- a set of example templates that you can only use if they match your real work.

To avoid vague or questionable claims, here are “credible but reviewable” example patterns—only use the parts you can back up:
- “I noticed X, proposed Y, and collaborated with Z to implement A; the outcome was B (or we improved C, based on D).”
- “I improved a process by doing C; this reduced [time/errors/rework] for [team/process], based on [any evidence].”
- “During a priority change, I coordinated timelines by updating stakeholders and delivering D by date E.”
- “I supported cross-team alignment by translating requirements into next steps; this avoided rework on [item].”

Send your details and any constraints from the internal application/interview rubric, and I’ll draft something that reads well without relying on assumptions about your true contributions."}
